title: A paradigm shift in understanding overuse running-related injuries: findings from the Garmin-RUNSAFE study point to a sudden not gradual onset
authors: Frandsen JSB, Simonsen NS, Hulme A, Jacobsen JS, Nielsen RO
population: English-speaking runners aged at least 18 years who were tracking running activities, 18-month follow-up (Garmin-RUNSAFE)
findings: Overload injury accounted for 467 of 1666 injuries (28%), while 1199 injuries were overuse (72%).
Among overuse injuries, the proportion of runners having a running-related problem before the injury was 6.9% (95% CI 5.5%-8.4%) 7 days prior and 11.1% (95% CI 9.4%-13.0%) 28 days prior.
Authors conclude most overuse injuries in adult runners may be classified as sudden repetitive overuse injuries rather than gradual-onset injuries.
limitations: Self-reported injuries and preceding problems; onset classification is subjective and depends on how often problems were reported; abstract gives no sample size of runners; not indexed in PubMed or Europe PMC on lookup, abstract taken from Crossref.
implications: Pain-trend check-ins would flag only a small fraction of overuse injuries ahead of time, so keep load-based guards (session-spike rule) as the primary mechanism and treat symptom check-ins as a secondary aid.
Supports checking each planned session against recent maxima rather than only slow weekly trends.
